canberra.title: Drivers beware! Stress balls are out to destroy your tyres
canberra.snippet: If you’re driving to and from Tuggeranong, you will need to keep your eyes peeled and focused on the road, but not for the reason y...
canberra.content:
A couple on an early morning walk found an ACT Policing branded stress ball with nails and screws driven through it. Photo: Lynda Bagnall.

If you’re driving to and from Tuggeranong, you will need to keep your eyes peeled and focused on the road, but not for the reason you might think.

Stress balls with ACT Policing branding have been found with screws and nails inserted into them on roads in Bonython, South Tuggeranong.

Many social media users joked about the branding on the ball, believing it to be a new contraption used by ACT Policing to stop speeding cars.

“Because of the rising cost of fuel, they sit on the roadside behind trees and throw rubber balls in front of speeding cars so when you hear a bump you slow down and check your tyres,” Martin Weber joked.

While some have seen the irony, others have expressed their concern about the potential damage they could cause.

Tuggeranong resident Lynda Bagnall was on a morning walk with her husband when she stumbled across one of the balls, leaving her shocked and appalled.

“We spotted it in the road. We picked it up and placed it in a safer place to take the pic,” Ms Bagnall said.

“We were quite alarmed and annoyed as it was obviously placed to cause a puncture, but thankfully haven’t seen any others.

“It’s awful to think that someone would even consider that a thing to do.”

Daisy Jing, from Rusden Europro Mechanics, said it is disappointing to hear of people deliberately trying to damage cars, but said it’s a good reminder for motorists to regularly check their tyres.

“It is common for nails and screw to accidentally pierce tyres in the ACT, especially when they drive around work sites,” Ms Jing said.

“For sedans going at high speeds, going over nails at high speeds will burst the tyres almost immediately.

“The bigger the car and the bigger the tyre, the less damage they will cause, but it’s still very important that you check consistently.

“When it comes to running over a nail, if the nail enters the side of the tyre, it means you will most likely need a replacement. If it enters the bottom where the tyre is thicker, that’s when we can remove it and fill it.

Ms Jing explained that apartment complexes are also common places for nail and screw punctures.

“Where there are a lot of people living with lots of work, the more likely there are for utes to accidentally drop them and cars to run over them,” she said.

“We’ve had a surprising number of calls from ANU as well.

“If you do notice your tyre deflating slowly or frequently, it is important to get it checked and not leave it that way. You don’t want the tyre to blow when you’re driving.”

ACT Police confirmed they are aware of online reports about stress balls being used as road hazards and are advising anyone who spots them, or similar objects, to report them.

“Should anyone have any information about the creation and placing of these items on ACT roads, they should contact Crime Stoppers via the Crime Stoppers ACT website.

“Information can be provided anonymously,” an ACT Policing spokesperson said.

canberra.title: Thousands of Canberrans can get onto full-fibre NBN connections by Christmas
canberra.snippet: About 2000 Canberra households can start switching their NBN copper connections to full fibre – and another 2000 are expected to be...
canberra.content:
Ventia splicer Dion Dickson upgrading a Holt home to access NBN fibre-to-the-premises. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

About 2000 Canberra households can start switching their NBN copper connections to full fibre – and another 2000 are expected to become eligible for the free upgrade by Christmas.

Holt, Narrabundah and Griffith are among the first suburbs to receive the new connection.

Construction has been underway since February to upgrade more than 38,000 ACT homes across 85 suburbs from fibre-to-the-node (FTTN) technology to fibre-to-the-premises (FTTP).

This is the first wave of a major investment to replace ageing FTTN copper connections with full fibre for around 97,000 homes and businesses across the Territory by 2030.

Federal Member for Fenner Andrew Leigh said this would give Canberrans better access to telehealth, online education and working-from-home options.

“The typical Canberra household is using over 500 gigabytes a month and has 25 connected devices – that’s forecast to rise to 44 connected devices by 2030,” he said.

“These gigabit speeds are crucially important in a modern economy … It will mean less time buffering and more time spent productively.”

Full-fibre connections can deliver speeds up to 18 times faster than the average copper broadband connection and are generally more reliable.

Canberrans will receive a letter informing them when their home is ready to be connected. Timelines and eligibility are also available online.

All homeowners then have to contact their preferred retail service provider to switch on the full fibre capability.

NBN infrastructure, planning and delivery manager Greg Thornton said the benefits went beyond faster internet speeds and greater reliability.

“[For example] in the Queensland floods … some of the areas that were still on copper [took] us up to 57 hours to replace,” he said.

“With fibre, if I look at the exact same scenario, it’s 1.5 hours that [it takes] for us to restore and give people back services … it’s a lot quicker to repair.”

Southsider Jim Thornton said switching from 5G to full fibre had made a huge difference to futureproofing his home and making internet access easier.

“I used to have Zoom meetings which would drop out previously,” he said.

“The speed is [now] there, the reliability is there … and we get better coverage.”

It also means providers can spend more time helping Canberrans upgrade rather than fixing copper lines.

Infinite Networks managing director Anthony Bortolotto said copper could even drop out when heavy rain reached the street pits.

“With more than half of Canberra working from home at least part of the week, this upgrade is long overdue,” he said.

“For internet providers, full fibre means our support team spends far less time managing weather faults on old copper lines and more time helping people get the best setup inside their homes.”

Mr Bortolotto explained the staged upgrades release by NBN also meant a city-wide backlog wouldn’t overwhelm the local workforce.

“Internet providers can process upgrade orders straight away. If the underground trenching from the street to your house is clear, the job is quick,” he explained.

“If tree roots or garden beds are in the path it needs to take, a crew will need to clear it first which can add a couple of weeks to the wait before Christmas.”

Homeowners are advised to plan where they’d like the connection box to go inside their house. The box needs to be near a power point on an inside wall, within a 12-metre radius from where the outside box is located.

Installers often put the box in the easiest spot at the front of the house or in the garage. A whole-home mesh Wi-Fi system can then make sure the fast speeds reach the back bedrooms and study.

Jim said the toughest aspect of upgrading was finding a retail service provider that would offer the type of deal he wanted.

Currently, many providers won’t allow you to switch unless you’re going onto a 100 megabit plan.

Mr Thornton said this would change around March 2027.

“What that means is, for customers who are cost conscious and actually want to stay on their existing speed plan, they can just migrate from copper straight across to fibre without upgrading,” he explained.

“[This is so] that people can take full advantage of an extra speed uplift.”

But for those who can’t wait, Jim had a workaround.

“If you have a plan, it’s installed for free; you cancel it at the end of the first month and then go to another provider that will actually sell you a plan at a lower speed,” he advised.

canberra.title: CPSU elections focussing on APS wages and conditions
canberra.snippet: Public servants’ wages are the overriding theme of the Community and Public Sector Union‘s national executive elections currently u...
canberra.content:
CPSU election candidates: Rebecca Fawcett, Christopher Warren and Amelio Sarchese. Photos: CPSU.

Public servants’ wages are the overriding theme of the Community and Public Sector Union‘s national executive elections currently underway.

Voting has started in the CPSU elections, with polls (postal ballots) closing for eligible members on 11 December.

Ballots formally opened on 6 November when the Australian Electoral Commission’s Industrial Elections and Ballots lodged ballot papers through Australia Post.

Those ballots are now arriving in letterboxes and CPSU members are beginning to make their decisions.

With the union in the thick of negotiations with the Australian Public Service Commission over APS wages and conditions, how much the Federal Government is willing to pay its workforce – and how hard the union is prepared to fight over it – has become the key CPSU election battleground.

Incumbent (and new) national secretary Rebecca Fawcett has hit the ground running, having already told the government to try harder over what it’s prepared to pay public servants.

More than 20,000 CPSU members recently took part in a snap poll the union conducted on the APSC’s first pay offer, with almost 90 per cent of participants rejecting it.

The APSC tabled a pay increase proposal of 9 per cent over three years, which comprises a 3.2 per cent rise from next March, then 3 per cent from March 2028, and 2.8 per cent in March 2029.

The package also included further measures to support greater consistency in pay across the APS.

Some workers in agencies with lower pay grades would get further salary increases of up to 0.5 per cent each year for three years (or a total of up to 1.5 per cent) to help close the pay gap between departments.

A new minimum pay point increase of 3 per cent was included for eligible employees progressing through their salary range where their existing advancement increase is lower than 3 per cent.

But the CPSU told the government its offer wasn’t good enough.

“CPSU members have delivered a clear message to the Commonwealth – we reject your pay offer,” Ms Fawcett said after this month’s membership poll.

In August, the union lodged a 15 per cent pay rise claim for APS staff, citing the need to lift the wages of the service’s lowest-paid workers.

The Federal Government has indicated that a 15 per cent pay rise over three years is highly unlikely.

Contesting the union’s national executive elections, rebel group Members United (Democracy 4 CPSU) is telling members they have a “historic opportunity” for change.

The group contested the union’s 2023 election, which was the first fully contested election in the CPSU since 2005.

The group’s campaign secured a third of the vote. This time they want to win a majority.

Members United’s candidate for national secretary, Christopher Warren, says the union’s current executive is not working hard enough to secure the best outcome for its members.

“No incumbent CPSU leadership team has been defeated this century. The result is a union still operating as it did in 2007, despite mounting threats to our job security and living standards,” he said.

“The CPSU leadership recommended management’s below-inflation pay deal to the membership in 2023.

“The long-run strategy of the CPSU leadership has catastrophically failed. These were supposed to be the years we recovered from the Abbott-Turnbull-Morrison era in public service real wages.

“Instead, they’ve failed to protect us from the inflation crisis, and now they’re unable to defend the basics with job cuts and the APSC proposing to cut basic conditions for a whole raft of agencies.

“The CPSU leadership simply have no plan to win above-inflation wage outcomes. But we do.”

Ms Fawcett has stated her experience and credentials as reasons CPSU should retain her as their national secretary.

“As CPSU’s legal director for 10 years, I oversaw major industrial and legal campaigns that have delivered real outcomes for members across the APS, broader public sector and private sector industries,” she has told the membership.

“I led the first round of APS-wide bargaining where we won groundbreaking working from home rights, expanded paid parental leave, stronger consultation rights, higher pay outcomes in lower-paid agencies, 25 per cent casual loading, and new leave entitlements that have made workplaces fairer and more flexible.”

CPSU member and workplace delegate Amelio Sarchese is also contesting the national secretary position, promising to “sort out APS bargaining and any lousy pay rise offers” and “put a stop” to political donations.

“I can assist members with flexible work arrangement requests, having researched the Fair Work Commission’s new broad powers to conciliate and arbitrate FWA disputes,” his election pitch states.

“I am here to help, and I will put members like you first.

“In the APS employee census, 10 per cent of 149,668 employee responses said ‘Yes’ to being subjected to bullying or harassment.

“If I am elected and if CPSU delegates/members are subjected to bullying and it doesn’t stop, I will fund a stop bullying order in the Fair Work Commission.

“Now, more than ever, with the high cost of living, it’s important that you elect someone who is working for you.”

canberra.title: Board of Inquiry into a decade of Indigenous deaths at AMC finally secures chair, start date
canberra.snippet: There’s finally a start date for a Board of Inquiry examination into Indigenous deaths at Canberra’s jail. The ACT Government...
canberra.content:
Joshua Creamer will chair the Board of Inquiry into Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander deaths at AMC. Photo: LinkedIn.

There’s finally a start date for a Board of Inquiry examination into Indigenous deaths at Canberra’s jail.

The ACT Government was meant to confirm a starting date in 2025 after Kurrajong independent MLA Thomas Emerson’s motion calling for an investigation into the number of Aboriginal people dying behind bars was unanimously passed in the Legislative Assembly.

Now it’s been announced that Waanyi and Kalkadoon man Joshua Creamer will chair the Board of Inquiry into Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander deaths in custody in the Alexander Maconochie Centre.

Corrections Minister Caitlin Tough said he brought significant legal expertise, leadership and deep understanding of issues affecting Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities to the investigation.

“Mr Creamer’s appointment reflects our government’s commitment to a trauma-informed and culturally sensitive inquiry, underpinned by independence, respect, and accountability,” she said.

“Mr Creamer brings extensive experience in human rights, the justice system and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander issues, with a strong track record in governance, community engagement and culturally informed inquiry processes.

“As chair, Mr Creamer will lead an inquiry that engages with the voices, experiences and perspectives of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.”

Mr Creamer is currently a barrister-at-law and has previously chaired the Truth-Telling and Healing Inquiry (QLD) and served as a barrister on the Queensland Child Safety Commission of Inquiry.

His expertise includes Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander engagement, cultural safety and truth-telling processes, human rights, native title, and a strong understanding of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander justice issues, informed by both lived and professional experience.

Mr Emerson said he was pleased significant resourcing had been allocated to the inquiry, while acknowledging some community members would be “frustrated that the start date is almost two years after my motion passed”.

“This comes after many years of pressure from family members who’ve lost loved ones in the AMC and from relentless First Nations community advocates including Julie Tongs and Joe Hedger, who’ve fought for scrutiny and justice on their behalf,” he said.

“It’s deplorable that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Canberrans with kin in the AMC have to worry about whether or not their loved ones will make it out alive.

“With powers similar to a Royal Commission, this Board of Inquiry offers an opportunity to uncover what’s really happening in the AMC and demand serious systemic reform.”

Canberra’s Indigenous community has been pushing for a Board of Inquiry ever since Steven Freeman’s death at the AMC in 2016.

Winnunga Nimmityjah CEO Julie Tongs previously said the acceptance to finally establish the inquiry was long overdue.

“Look what’s happened since … we’ve had more deaths in custody,” she said.

“[This] gives the mothers, our men and women and our community some hope that in time things will change.”

The Board of Inquiry will examine issues that could be contributing to the deaths of Indigenous people behind bars.

These include the availability and effectiveness of rehabilitation, support and advocacy services (including those delivered by non-government organisations) and assess whether the AMC’s legislative, policy and oversight frameworks, complaints mechanisms, staff training, restrictive practices, accountability arrangements and organisational culture adequately meet the needs of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander detainees.

Health care and mental health support, substance misuse, institutional or structural racism, cultural safety and human rights, and social, historic and economic factors are all issues to also be considered.

The Board of Inquiry will consider the deaths of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people at AMC since 2016. It will also consider the death in custody of a detainee who died in NSW custody two years after being transferred from the Territory.

Despite hopes the investigation would begin this year, the board will commence on 25 February 2027.

It will run for six months.

The board’s final report must be provided to the Chief Minister by 25 August 2027.

A full breakdown of the terms of reference is available online.

canberra.title: Prosecutors will appeal teen rapist’s sentence that shocked community
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to sexual abuse. Prosecutors will appeal the community-based sentence a teenage boy received after h...
canberra.content:
The now-18-year-old teenager was handed a suspended sentence for sexual assault. Photo: John Lomnicki.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to sexual abuse.

Prosecutors will appeal the community-based sentence a teenage boy received after he was spared jail for brutally and repeatedly raping a young woman.

The boy was 16, nearly 17, when he went to a Canberra house party in mid-2025 and met the 18-year-old woman, Region has previously reported.

They left the party, walked to a nearby green belt and began kissing consensually.

But he then got on top of her and forcefully and violently raped her numerous times over about 20 minutes.

The teen, who pleaded guilty to a charge of sexual intercourse without consent, was born in South Asia and moved to Australia to be with his family at the start of 2025.

While he said he was “sickened” by his actions, he also told the author of a court report that the woman was “exaggerating stuff” and that he “didn’t force her to do that and this”.

When sentencing him in October 2026, Justice Andrew Muller took into account his young age, low risk of reoffending, lack of prior sexual experience, restricted opportunity for social development due to only recently moving to Australia, and the need to promote his rehabilitation.

“What is clear is he now realises the giving of consent to sexual interaction necessarily involves clear and active communications to that effect, not just an absence of express refusal,” Justice Muller said.

“I accept his prior lack of sexual experience and inevitably limited insight into societal norms in Australia given his very short time in the country before the offending are factors mitigating his moral culpability.”

The teen, who legally cannot be named due to his age, was sentenced to 18 months’ jail, fully suspended for a good behaviour order.

The sentencing was followed by extensive outrage in the media and online commentary.

Region has now confirmed that the ACT Director of Public Prosecutions has lodged an appeal against the boy’s sentence.

The appeal hearing is unlikely to take place before the second half of 2027.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call Triple Zero.

If you have been affected by sexual violence, or someone you know has, you can report it to police by attending a police station or phoning 131 444.

australia.title: What’s behind Australia’s surge in teen extremism?
australia.snippet: Young people are being found with ‘hard drives full of what can only be described as gore’, one expert says In March, Guardian Australia ...
australia.content:
In March, Guardian Australia revealed that most people who have been charged with the new federal crime of possession of violent extremist material are under 18.

This week Australian federal police sounded the alarm about a surge in teen extremism: 32 of the 37 young people prosecuted in counter-terrorism cases since 2020 were charged in the past two years.

The growth in youth extremism is happening within a sprawling online ecosystem. My investigations have tracked the rise of online networks that urge violence and nihilism for their own sake, in which perpetrators coerce victims not much younger than themselves to commit brutal and degrading acts.

In a review of 55 youth terrorism cases, the AFP has found that the profile is mixed. They are often young men. Many have received some support or intervention for a mental health condition. Some are from stable homes, others not.

What they have most in common is that they are young people on the internet. Experts say the age of those caught up in these crimes is decreasing.

In the last month two teenagers in Darwin have been charged with collecting documents that could facilitate acts of terrorism.

The second teenager was arrested after an initial examination of documents and electronic devices at a Northern Territory home, according to the AFP, allegedly found material and online discussions “including glorification of mass casualty attacks at schools”.

The arrests came five months after another NT teenager was charged with making posts with “pro-Nazi, anti-immigration, anti-trans and white nationalist themes”. The charge sheet alleges he also possessed videos of white nationalist terrorist attacks, including the 2019 Christchurch mosque shooting and the 2022 Buffalo shooting that it partly inspired.

All matters are still before the courts.

Experts involved in harm prevention programs, including the Victoria University professor Debra Smith, have watched the age of this cohort decrease dramatically over the past decade.

Instead of considering the challenge exclusively through the lens of radicalisation, Smith says we need to recognise that some young people are being socialised and finding identity in online spaces that may appear exciting and transgressive but are ultimately harmful to themselves, and may encourage them to do harm to others.

She has seen cases where teenagers are being found with “hard drives full of what can only be described as gore”.

“It’s like getting involved in any other … unhealthy subcultural aspect of life … [such as] gangs or crime for payment,” she says. “There’s this offering of what young people can look at and get involved in that just simply wasn’t there years ago.”

The Guardian’s investigation into the growth of extremist material charges, as well as the surge of young people in Australia ensnared in sadistic online extortion and gore networks, reveals an amorphous online ecosystem in which young people may easily come into contact with extreme and violent content.

A teenager in New South Wales who pleaded guilty to possessing violent extremist material, among other charges, described how he first came across such content on TikTok when he was 14 and sought validation by talking to others online. He used ChatGPT to research the Boston marathon bomber Dzhokhar Tsarnaev as well as security arrangements at the Sydney Opera House. He was sentenced to a three-year community corrections order.

Others have told police how they became involved in so-called “gore” channels on Telegram, where more and more extreme footage – including of animal abuse –is traded.

Given the age of many involved, Levi West, a research fellow at the Australian National University, says they may be considered as much victims as perpetrators, which is a significant challenge for how authorities respond.

It’s important for parents, schools and others to think about what’s sitting underneath the uptick in numbers, he says, and not just the “algorithms”. He points to the legacies of Covid-19 and lockdowns as well as the presence of screens and digital technologies in the lives of young people.

“We are not going to arrest our way out of this problem,” West says.

With people as young as 13 before the courts, Australia must consider if authorities are taking the right approach and have the right resources for this challenge.

The Guardian’s investigation into the possession of extremist material charges in South Australia and around the country found that many of those who had been before the courts faced a range of health and social difficulties, including autism diagnoses and learning challenges – and raised questions about whether some young people understand a crime has been committed.

Smith has seen many young people caught up in these activities who come from troubled family backgrounds, while others have had every opportunity in life.

There is a role for everyone involved in caring for young people, she says, from parents and schools to sporting clubs, to recognise when someone might be engaging in harmful behaviours long before there is a risk of violence, then help them access non-punitive pathways for help.

“It’s really important to understand it through a developmental lens – that these are young people who are making decisions with young brains,” Smith says.

“My grave concern is that if we are just giving everyone terrorism offences at [age] 12, 13, 14, 15, we’re starting to label them the thing that they will become.”

australia.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon takes the stand - podcast
australia.snippet: After seven weeks of intense public interest, former police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon has entered the witness box to give his testimony...
australia.content:
After seven weeks of intense public interest, former police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon has entered the witness box to give his testimony of how Jesse Baird and Luke Davies died.

Facing cross-examination, Lamarre-Condon told the court he was guilty of manslaughter, but denies he intentionally murdered the pair in February 2024.

Reporter Kat Wong joins Taylah Strano to unpack the tense courtroom exchanges and what happens next in the high-profile trial

australia.title: New allegations against convicted rapist Ralph Carr revealed: ‘I was blacking out while saying no’
australia.snippet: Exclusive: Former staffers detail unwanted sexual advances by Melbourne talent manager who was this year found guilty of raping an ex-emp...
australia.content:
When Sophie* started working at Ralph Carr Management just after her 21st birthday, she thought she had landed her dream job: red carpet events, celebrity clients, even international travel.

Sophie had been hired as an intern in RCM’s Melbourne office in the mid-2010s and, before long, she had deferred her degree in film and television to work there full-time. Within months, her hard work had paid off: Carr had invited her on a trip to LA with a high-profile client.

“I’m nervous but excited!!” she texted a friend as soon as she landed.

“It’ll be the best experience of your life,” her friend replied.

Within two days, that excitement had turned to trauma and shame: “I feel violently ill at all of this,” she messaged another friend hours after allegedly being assaulted by her boss, who was then 55. “Just gonna try and forget.”

In August Carr was sentenced to six years in jail after being found guilty of raping a former employee in 2023, when she was in her 20s and he was 66. He pleaded not guilty and has lodged an appeal.

The week after he was found guilty, Guardian Australia published the allegations of dozens of former female employees accusing Carr of verbally abusive and intimidating behaviour in the workplace dating back to the 90s, with several also accusing him of sexual harassment. He denied the allegations.

Sophie was part of that investigation – but there is more to her story. Today she is joined by two more women who are coming forward to the Guardian with new allegations of unwanted physical sexual advances by Carr, in incidents dating from the mid-2000s and all involving women in their early 20s.

In an email to the Guardian, Carr’s lawyer said the allegations “are historic in nature and unsupported by any evidence whatsoever. Our client has no recollection that factual circumstances as alleged ever took place and vehemently denies that they did.”

The Guardian understands there is an ongoing police inquiry involving Carr. A spokesperson confirmed that Victoria police are investigating an alleged sexual assault in Melbourne in 2005 and said: “As investigations are ongoing it would be inappropriate to comment further.”

‘Pushing me and holding me down’

Sophie alleges that Carr assaulted her not long after she landed in LA. After a work dinner with him, she met up for drinks with her friend Mel* in Beverly Hills. Mel was there with two others and afterwards all four went to the bar of a Hollywood hotel where they met up with Carr.

At some point, Carr invited everybody up to his suite. And at a later point, everyone else left.

“I was shitfaced, obviously,” says Sophie, who remembers only snippets of what followed. “I’ve only had this feeling before when I’ve been put under for a procedure, when you feel the world rush around you – it felt like that, and he was pushing me and holding me down, kissing me and grabbing my crotch.

“The last thing I remember is me blacking out while I was saying no, and he was pushing me down.” He touched her over the top of her underwear, she says, but she doesn’t remember being penetrated. The next morning she woke up in Carr’s bed, naked but for his T-shirt, “my clothes and underwear on the floor, covered in vomit”.

A series of text messages that night show how concerned her friend had been about leaving Sophie alone with Carr. Mel wrote:

Sophie replied: “Hah I’m okay?” – but 23 minutes later, her texts became garbled: “All yo” and “D”, and then “Henge alllllll too or good”.

Carr was in the suite’s living area when Sophie woke up in his bed the next morning. She threw up in the toilet, found her clothes and dressed quickly, and was down the hotel hallway when he called her back. “He said, ‘You forgot something’ and he’s holding up my underwear,” she says. “He had the most fucked look in his eyes.”

Sophie ended up locked outside the Airbnb she had meant to stay in that night and texted Mel again while she waited to be let in:

The women talked on the phone and later texted again. “I think he just tried to kiss me,” Sophie texted. “And was feeling me up.” Looking back, Sophie says she was trying to laugh it off.

“I told him this morning that I don’t remember anything from being up at his room,” Sophie wrote to Mel. “Which is true. But I remember him leaning in to kiss me. And getting me. And me being like nooooooooo. Hahahah.”

Mel replied:

“That email” was sent by hotel staff to Sophie the next morning, describing “an issue we had last night” in Carr’s suite. A noise complaint had been made by the guests in the neighbouring room, which shared a locked adjoining door. They said somebody had tried to get through that door.

“Either Mr. Carr or his guest was banging on the connecting door and trying to get into the connecting room and saying, ‘Let me in! Let me in!’. Obviously, the guests that were staying in the connecting room were very scared and upset about the situation.”

Carr got Sophie to reply:

“I’ve just spoken to Ralph about this. Apparently there was a prom after party on the other side of the neighbours with lots of high school kids … Ralph and his guests have said it was one of the high school kids that was yelling this and definitely not him or his guests.”

The staff member replied that the guests who were complaining only had one adjoining door, and that it connected to “the suite that Ralph is in”. Carr was charged a $250 fee. The hotel has not responded to questions from the Guardian.

Sophie will never know exactly what happened or if it was her banging on the door that night – but, she tells the Guardian, there are moments she remembers.

“I don’t feel like I was raped … but he definitely touched me, and he definitely hovered over me, definitely held me down, I definitely said no,” she says. “I definitely woke up in his T-shirt, [otherwise] fully naked with my clothes on the other side of the room.”

Mel wasn’t the only friend Sophie messaged after the alleged assault; that afternoon, LA time, she also messaged her best friend, Jenna*, back home, over Facebook.

With Jenna, there was less laughter.

Sophie And then I woke up naked in his t shirt

Sophie And I’m hope the only reason that that happened was because I vommed on everything

Sophie I just don’t no why I didn’t have undies on and that scares the fuck out of me

Sophie spent at least another year at Ralph Carr Management, weathering the alleged daily abuse and toxic workplace revealed by the Guardian in August. She remembers Carr yelling and swearing at his young female staff and demanding they be on call 24/7.

She says she would have to race to his desk when he shouted her name, and bend over him and type emails for him in such uncomfortably close proximity that she could feel his legs touching her.

Still, she stayed in the job. As a 21-year-old, she says, she had more creative power and opportunities than most her age. “He’d actually trust my opinion,” she says. “And he wasn’t as evil to me as he was to the others. I don’t know if he generally liked me better, or if it was because of the incident, or if, in his idea of the workplace, [having favourites] was a tactic.”

A year after the LA trip, she was finally considering quitting. “I honestly don’t know how I stayed this long,” she texted Mel. “Especially after everything that happened in LA…”

She questioned whether she could have been given a sleeping pill or drugged on the night in question, to which Mel replied: “I mean, you were pretty drunk.”

Sophie continued: “Yeah I was fucked but not fucked enough to wake up naked in my boss’s bed (that was covered in vom) with the last memory of the night was me being fully clothed yelling no no get off me as he was literally on top of me kissing me and touching me on the fan.”

In the same exchange, Mel tried to urge Sophie to tell someone – and to finally quit: “Can’t let him get away with his abuse.”

Sophie never went to a doctor for a toxicology test to see if there were drugs in her system. She ended up losing hair from stress. “It definitely impacted me psychologically,” she says. “Feeling something bad happened, and I’ll never know what happened.”

She spoke to Australian police about that night in 2025, after hearing about the rape allegation for which Carr was convicted – but given that the alleged assault took place in a different jurisdiction, they told her there was nothing they could do.

Sophie’s mother remembers how much that time affected her daughter. “She was so excited to get her dream job in such a hotly contested field,” she says.

But the cracks didn’t take long to appear. “She said to me, ‘Mum I’ve got my dream job and the worst boss in the world.’ But to me it felt like she could handle him.”

It would take years for Sophie to tell her mother about that night in LA. “We were sitting in the car,” she says. “She burst into tears. I burst into tears … It’s every mother’s nightmare. And everyone knows what women go through when they accuse someone in that type of field.”

After Carr was convicted of rape, Sophie’s mother was horrified when the former Australian rules footballer Sam Newman suggested that the young victim may have had “buyer’s remorse”. “No wonder sexual assault victims are so reluctant to go and relive the trauma through the courts,” she says.

‘I’d given him no sign that I was interested’

Sophie’s was the latest allegation of assault heard by the Guardian. One of the earliest dates back to 2006, when Tess, who was 22 and is using her first name only, experienced the first of two unwanted sexual advances from Carr, then 46.

It was the Australia Day weekend, and Tess met up with Carr and her friend Caitlin*, who was seeing one of Carr’s acquaintances at the time. After drinks one night the group went back to Carr’s Clifton Street house for more.

At some point, Caitlin and her date went to Carr’s guesthouse, leaving Carr and Tess alone. Tess remembers what allegedly happened next as “disgusting”.

“He just disappeared and then came [back] around the corner only in his undies,” she says. “I’d given him no sign that I was interested in him. He came and climbed on top of me. It was gross. Gross.”

She told him no, she says, and went home soon afterwards. The next morning, when Caitlin asked Tess where she had gone, Tess told Caitlin what had happened.

“We were like, ‘He’s absolutely disgusting,’” Caitlin remembers of the discussion. “This man was … so much older than us.”

On Whatsapp in 2015, the pair remembered the night:

Tess wasn’t more than tipsy that night and managed to get away – but she was “very drunk” when Carr took her and Caitlin to Love Machine, a Melbourne nightclub, a month or so later.

“He walked straight into the nightclub, knew everyone on the door, made you feel VIP,” Tess says. “He’s looking after us, I’m not going to do anything to be ungrateful.”

That’s why, she thinks, he talked her into going to a part of the building that she believes was not accessible to the public. “There was no one down there – he was trying to kiss me, and tried to put his hands down my pants, and I laughed it off. I didn’t feel scared – but I didn’t ask for him to touch me.”

He got to the top of her underwear inside her pants, she alleges. “He tried to have a grope around, and I pulled him out.” They went back to the main area of the club and Tess told Caitlin what had happened.

“We just laughed over it,” Tess says now. “Like, ‘Yuck. What a creepy old guy.’ But yeah, I got out – and it’s horrible to read about people that did not.”

‘I was just like a shell of a human’

Kayla, who is using her first name only, was 22 in 2014 when she started working for Carr, by now in his mid-50s; she experienced the same bullying, intimidation and toxic workplace culture detailed previously. “Any time he was coming into the office everyone would shit themselves,” she says. Looking back, she finds his volatility “ridiculous” but “at the time it was petrifying”.

“He used to just sit back and you had to stand between his fucking knees and the keyboard,” she remembers. “I’m a small person but like, yeah. It was just not nice.”

The first time she felt uncomfortable with him was on a Sunday night, shortly after she started.

Carr had invited her to the Bridge hotel with a group to watch a client perform in a televised talent show – but when she got there, it was just the two of them. “I was naive, you know? … I’d only just started working there.”

Her boss paid for her drinks – Kayla says lots of them – and then offered to drive her to the train station, which was near the office. He stopped there and asked her to join him for a nightcap, which she declined. He needed to pick something up and she says he told her not to look in the glovebox while he was gone, allegedly saying that there were drugs in there.

“It was like he was just trying to bait me into wanting to have a good night,” she says. “He was just being super bizarre.” She remembers him leaning his arm on her leg in the car at one point; he wasn’t forceful, she says: “I think he was testing the waters of what he could get away with.”

When Carr returned to the car, she told him she could just catch a train home; he gave her $50 for a cab instead. On the drive, she texted her housemate Jacquie, who is also using only her first name, telling her that he had hit on her.

The next day, Kayla says, “he treated me like absolute dirt at work. Just so, so abusive.”

Still, she stayed in the job: “I assumed that this was what the music industry was and you just had to put up with it.” But at that year’s Christmas party, hosted in his home with lots of alcohol and drugs available, she alleges that he tried again.

She remembers asking to use the bathroom; after he showed her there, he followed her in and grabbed her by the waist from behind. When he “crept his hands up towards the front of my chest”, she says, she flipped around before he reached her breasts and told him to get out.

He played it off as though there’d been a miscommunication and at first she let herself believe it. “I don’t know,” she explains, “you’re inebriated, and someone’s being nice to you for the first time in months.”

So when Carr invited her to see the upstairs of the house, she followed him. But this time “it was definitely clear that he was trying to do the wrong thing”.

When he got to the bedroom, “I was like, ‘Oh, fuck, here we go,’” she says. He put his arm around her, she says, and went to guide her in – but she said no and stayed at the door. His wife was pregnant at the time. He sat on his bed and pleaded with her, saying, “No one’s going to know.”

“I didn’t want to lose my job so I wasn’t telling him to fuck off or making a scene. I was just like, ‘No, I’m not comfortable’ … It was so far-fetched from reality. At what point did he think that was going to happen?”

She left that party unharmed but the workplace bullying worsened – and its impact on her was significant.

“I started drinking two bottles of wine before bed just to try and get to sleep because I was so anxious … Mum and Dad were fucking freaking out, and it was just terrible. I ended up getting a bald patch and I was down to, like, 48 kilos.”

Her friend Jacquie remembers this too: “When she got the job she was so excited,” she says. “It was so noticeable by the end how much he tore her character apart. She was a shell of herself by the time she got out of there.”

Kayla first spoke to the Guardian in 2018, at the beginning of an eight-year investigation, but she contacted police in January 2025 after she heard about the rape allegation against Carr, and detailed some of her alleged experiences over email in the hope she could support the victim.

On coming forward with her story now, she says: “I got out relatively lucky in comparison … It was traumatic at the time. But when you know so many other people went through it, and when you understand he’s a predator and it wasn’t you in particular … I feel very validated.”

*Names have been changed

  • Do you know more? Contact Steph Harmon steph.harmon@theguardian.com

  • Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse is available at Full Stop Australia. Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

australia.title: Icac’s drama and dirt files show NSW’s ‘guns for hire’ problem. But neither major party is serious about reform
australia.snippet: Chris Minns is trying to address the threat of undeclared lobbying but falls well short of what the commission recommended five years ago...
australia.content:
A dirt file on a state minister peddled to journalists. A subterranean campaign to discredit the building commissioner. Convincing the Liberal party to unseat councillors in the Hills district who were blocking a developer.

The New South Wales corruption watchdog’s recent inquiry, Rosny, revealed the ease with which the key protagonists – a group of rightwing Liberal operatives known as the Reformers, all of whom were former staffers – could move along the corridors of NSW parliament.

The Independent Commission against Corruption (Icac) has alleged that, unbeknown to their fellow Liberals, the operatives – including the then treasurer, Dominic Perrottet’s own brother Charles Perrottet – were being paid $2m by one of NSW’s most notorious developers, Jean Nassif, and that they worked to progress his interests.

Only one of the rightwing operatives involved in the Rosny inquiry was a registered lobbyist and subject to rules about declaring his clients and keeping records of interactions with ministers.

Yet all of them were on first name terms with many of their former colleagues and bureaucrats, affording them easy access for a chin-wag or to mix with powerful players – especially within the Liberal party’s machine.

Nassif – who told Icac he was “not corrupt” – has fled to Lebanon after the collapse of his company Toplace, leaving hundreds of buyers with substandard buildings. Charles Perrottet has repeatedly denied taking payments from Nassif for political outcomes. Dominic Perrottet is not a person of interest in Icac’s inquiry and is not accused of any wrongdoing.

The issue of access for former staffers – whether they be third-party lobbyists employed by specialist lobbying firms who are “guns for hire”, or “government relations” specialists employed directly by companies or industry groups – has long been a concern for Icac.

As Rosny showed, there was no way politicians could know who some of these figures were working for because these were allegedly undeclared guns for hire.

The NSW Labor government has now introduced a bill to clarify obligations for at least one class of lobbyist: the guns for hire. It passed the lower house on Wednesday, though it may not become law before the election.

Chris Minns’ efforts to address the threat that undeclared lobbying poses fall well short of what Icac recommended five years ago.

First, the good bits of the proposed legislation.

It would formally establish the NSW Electoral Commission as the regulator of third party lobbyists and bolster its investigative powers to audit compliance with the Lobbying of Government Officials Act and lobbyists code of conduct.

Icac recommended a separate lobbying commissioner but, given the electoral commission already has responsibility for the register, Minns has proposed it get the job.

“Third-party lobbyists are already subject to information and disclosure obligations, including disclosing information to the electoral commission for publication on the lobbyists register,” the special minister of state, John Graham, told Guardian Australia.

“The bill would allow the NSW Electoral Commission to audit compliance of third-party lobbyists and require relevant accounts, documents, information and explanations.”

It also extends the act to third party lobbyists interacting with councils. Lobbyists interacting with councils will need to register and adhere to the code. This had been identified by Icac as a gap that needed fixing.

But the bill also has bad bits. It ignores some of Icac’s most important recommendations.

The most glaring loophole is that the disclosure regime doesn’t extend to staff employed directly by companies – usually with a title like “government relations” or “corporate affairs” – even through they also lobby politicians.

These individuals make up about 80% of the people floating round the corridors of power. Most are former political staff members.

Graham said registering in-house lobbyists would have “created unnecessary red tape given it is already clear whose interests are being served or represented, and ministerial diary disclosures provide transparency of lobbyists’ interaction”.

This ignores the need for record keeping under the lobbyist regulations. If inhouse lobbyists were subject to the rules, they would be obliged to keep records of who they lobbied, as would the ministers and bureaucrats who were approached.

The government argues it plans to enhance ministerial diary disclosures, to make them fully searchable, rather than issuing them quarterly in pdf form.

The legislation will also clarify that third party lobbyists will need to disclose attendance at fundraising events involving exclusive or private access to a minister.

But the bill does not extend to lobbyists’ interactions with key ministerial staff, such as their chief of staff – which Operation Rosny demonstrated were important conduits to the minister.

“We’re regulating ministers and senior public servants because they’re decision makers. Ministerial staff are not decision makers,” Graham said.

Chiefs of staff can be almost as powerful as their minister, because they control access – and can direct policy staff.

Operation Rosny heard allegations about how the Liberal operatives, in their quest to smear the reputation of the building commissioner, provided material to a chief of staff, who then passed it to the chief of staff for the minister responsible for the building commissioner. The Liberal figures denied to Icac they were seeking to remove the building commissioner on behalf of Nassif.

Icac also heard evidence that Charles Perrottet talked to ministers directly about the building commissioner. He was not a registered lobbyist, yet he enjoyed extraordinary access and influence.

Neither the chiefs of staff nor the ministers were aware that Charles Perrottet was being paid by Nassif via a lobbying firm.

The government has also watered down Icac’s proposals for a six-month prohibition on certain public service roles taking on lobbying roles in either lobbying firms or private enterprise when leaving the bureaucracy.

Icac wanted certain sensitive roles to require six months’ “gardening leave” – as occurs when public servants leave the state’s gambling regulator.

If the bill ever reaches the upper house – and its future is now uncertain – debate is likely to be feisty.

The Greens have introduced a private member’s bill into parliament that would implement most of Icac’s recommendations from five years ago – including extending the lobbyists scheme to inhouse lobbyists.

Kobi Shetty, the minor party’s anti-corruption spokesperson, said her bill would have included a four-year exclusion for some public sector employees.

“When industries with deep pockets get a louder voice than the communities affected by their decisions, public trust in our democracy is eroded,” Shetty says.

The Centre for Public Integrity senior counsel Geoffrey Watson says the government’s bill is a step in the right direction and he hopes it passes the Legislative Council.

But he wishes the government had been more ambitious.

australia.title: NSW’s latest news Instagram account has an unlikely group behind it: the Labor party
australia.snippet: Expert warns of ‘huge loophole in political communication laws’ as state government among parties presenting accounts as unaffiliated new...
australia.content:
“Breaking,” a reel from the Instagram account nswnewsroom reads. “Another Liberal MP quits, almost a third now gone.”

The post looks like it could have been made by a media outlet. It cites the source as the Daily Telegraph and Jordan Lane, a New South Wales MP, who is the sixth sitting Liberal member to announce they won’t re-contest their seat at the March 2027 election.

But the account’s bio tells a different story: it was authorised by the NSW Labor state secretary.

The account, which first posted two weeks ago and says “keep up to date with with [sic] news from NSW govt” in its bio, is part of an increasingly common tactic where Australian political parties set up accounts that appear at first glance to be unaffiliated news sources. The accounts feature different names and imagery without prominent party branding, to promote specific messages or highlight their own side.

Andrew Hughes, an expert in political marketing at the Australian National University, said these types of accounts take advantage of a “huge loophole in our political communication laws in Australia when it comes to digital and social media communications”.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

“More and more of us get our news and information primarily from digital and social media,” said Hughes.

“There’s more and more potential for that information to be used against voters who aren’t engaged with politics or the news to a really good level of detail to spot disinformation and misinformation,” he said.

As unpaid content, the posts are not subject to the same authorisation requirements as paid advertisements at state and federal level. In NSW, an authorisation in the account profile or a website directly linked to that post is acceptable. The nswnewsroom account added its authorisation after reporting by the Sydney Morning Herald.

A spokesperson for the NSW government referred Guardian Australia to a statement shared with the paper, which said the page was “a Labor-affiliated social media page, consistent with the practices of most major political parties and a number of minor parties across Australia”.

In Victoria a similar account, vicnewstoday, was set up ahead of this month’s Victorian state election. While the account bio contains an authorisation by Victorian Labor HQ, the posts, including videos of Ben Carroll and ministers at press conferences, do not. In one, captioned “BREAKING: Liberals did a deal with ‘the most anti-worker party’”, Carroll criticises a preference deal between the Liberals and One Nation.

In late October, the Labor party launched a page titled “Don’t Risk It Vic”, promoting posts that raise concerns about an alliance between the Liberal and One Nation parties.

Meta’s ad library reveals that page was the highest-spending political advertiser in the country last week, paying $67,138 to promote its posts between 31 October and 6 November.

A spokesperson for the Victorian Labor Party said social media was “an important way to communicate with Victorians where they are, particularly those who don’t engage with traditional media”.

“There is a lot at stake for Victoria. And everyone deserves to hear the facts about what a Liberal-One Nation government would mean for our health system, schools, police and cost-of-living.”

Monica Attard, former Media Watch host, now professor of journalism practice at the University of Technology, Sydney, said in an age where social media was “awash with deepfakes”, it was “really important for consumers – and probably equally important for political parties – to disclose clearly and always”.

“I would think that the possibility of misuse or tampering would be relatively high.”

Ahead of the 2025 federal election, Guardian Australia uncovered a string of similar social media pages set up by Labor, the Coalition, Climate 200 and campaign group Advance.

All pages carried basic authorisation messages from their creators, but the page names and profile pictures did not immediately denote the source. Labor state divisions in NSW and Western Australia set up at least two anti-Peter Dutton pages, with posts raising doubts about health spending and WA’s GST deal under a Coalition government.

The Liberal party launched a page called “Teals Revealed”, scrutinising the voting record of Climate 200-backed independents, while Climate 200, in turn, set up “Independent News”, to promote news about crossbench MPs.

world.title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza cleared of using AI to write prize-winning story
world.snippet: After a month-long investigation it was concluded that Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which won the £10,000 Caine prize, was ‘human-...
world.content:
The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation.

Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October.

Five days later, the Atlantic published an article titled “Yet another literary prize winner seems to be AI”, in which the author and journalist Vauhini Vara said the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated.

The Caine prize chair, Ellah Wakatama, said in a statement: “From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human-written. We now look forward to awarding and celebrating Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza … before the end of the year.”

She said: “When concerns were raised, we have a duty as an organisation to look at them carefully and fairly,” adding that the prize had taken a “human-centred” approach to its investigation.

“Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel and The Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published,” Wakatama said. “It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author.”

Kundizeza, who had strongly denied using generative AI to write the story, said he was “relieved” that the allegations had been dismissed after the investigation. “It was not necessary in the first place, I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey,” he said.

Vara’s article prompted outrage online, with many claiming that Black writers, and Africans in particular, were being unfairly singled out by allegations of the use of AI.

Associated Press contributed to this report

world.title: Lewis Hamilton visits Egypt’s Rafah crossing and Gaza aid facilities
world.snippet: Seven-time F1 world champion tours border area and logistics warehouses operated by Egyptian Red Crescent Lewis Hamilton has visited Egyp...
world.content:
Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip to meet organisations sending humanitarian aid to the territory.

The seven-time Formula One world champion has spoken out about conflict and humanitarian crises in the region, and has called for peace. He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire.

“I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage,” Hamilton said in October.

A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.

Israeli forces have continued to advance, expanding their control from 53% of the territory to at least 60%, an independent commission of UN experts said last month.

Airstrikes also continue, and Israeli fire along the advancing front has killed at least 196 Palestinians, including 18 women, 32 boys and 11 girls, the commission said.

Hamilton toured Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with Gaza before visiting logistics warehouses operated by the Egyptian Red Crescent, which facilitates the entry of aid to Gaza.

At the crossing, Hamilton greeted aid workers with “Assalamu alaikum” a widely used Arabic greeting meaning “peace be upon you.” He shook hands and briefly spoke to workers and officials.

Khaled Megawer, the governor of North Sinai, where Rafah is located, said the visit was intended to help Hamilton learn about Egypt’s efforts to send aid to Gaza.

The visit comes after Hamilton made his 400th race start on Sunday at the São Paulo Grand Prix at Interlagos.

The first black F1 driver, he made his debut with McLaren in 2007. He is only the second F1 driver to start 400 races after his former teammate Fernando Alonso, who achieved the milestone in 2024.

world.title: Collision of two trains in Egypt kills at least seven
world.snippet: President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 50km from Cairo Seven people were killed and...
world.content:
Seven people were killed and at least 125 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said.

The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 50km (30 miles) south of Cairo, when a train travelling to Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry.

An inspection indicated that the Cairo-Aswan train had been stationary on the same track, officials said.

The health ministry gave the casualty toll, adding more than 70 of the injured were discharged after receiving treatment.

Train derailments and crashes are common in Egypt, where the railway system has a history of mismanagement and poor maintenance of equipment. In recent years the government has announced modernisation initiatives to improve its railways.

Ayman Gamal, a resident of Kafr Girza in al-Ayyat where the crash occurred, said people rushed to the scene, pulled out survivors and called ambulances.

Gamal said he saw about 80 of the injured being taken by ambulances to hospital. Some passengers were trapped inside one of the carriages of the stationary train and died, he said.

Egypt’s president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said in a social media post that he had ordered a prompt investigation.

Outside al-Wasta central hospital in Beni Suef province, where some of the injured were taken for treatment, survivors said passengers were in shock and struggling to breathe because of all the dust that was kicked up. Nearby villagers eventually got them out, they said.

Farha Gamal, a survivor who was inside the Fayyoum train, said she saw some of the passengers who appeared dead and others were struggling to find their way out of the car. “There were other cars that were completely mangled,” she said in an interview.

Emergency teams and cranes were dispatched to the crash site to clear the wreckage and restore train services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, the Egyptian railway authority said.

Last September, a train driver and his assistant were injured after two freight trains collided in the same district.

Egypt’s deadliest train crash was in 2002 when more than 300 people were killed after a fire broke out on an overnight train journeying from Cairo to southern Egypt.

world.title: How African philosophies inspired a new approach to staging film festivals in Manchester
world.snippet: See My World, an event highlighting the pan-African thought via film, poetry and dance, builds on momentum sparked by local activists and...
world.content:
African philosophies including exploring how lessons from the past can shape the present and near future have inspired a film festival coming to Manchester.

See My World, a day dedicated to independent creators from across the African diaspora in the north of England, will take place at the Contact theatre on 21 November.

The festival is part of See My World’s year-round programme showcasing pan-African arts, culture and events.

It reflects the determination among creatives and activists in Manchester to build on the legacy of the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester – which connected luminaries of postwar independence movements with a shared vision of liberation – after last year’s 80th anniversary commemorations.

See My World’s CEO and artistic director, Tunde Adekoya, said this month’s film festival was taking inspiration from across the spectrum of pan-African thought, including the works of Kenyan writers John Mbiti, an Anglican theologian who died in 2019, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, the author of the groundbreaking 1986 book Decolonising the Mind who died last year.

Both writers rejected the colonial conceit that African thought was inferior, stressed the importance of community and saw reclaiming African ways of knowing as essential to a people’s self-understanding.

While Mbiti sought common ground between African religions and Christianity, Ngũgĩ was a Marxist. He argued colonialism was motivated by cultural and economic conquest, and that European powers used language as their sharpest instrument. Ngũgĩ famously abandoned English to write in Gikuyu, a Bantu language mainly spoken in Kenya and criticised the role missionary Christianity played in colonial rule.

Adekoya said: “It’s a day dedicated to pan-African and global majority films from the north of England with exclusive premieres of documentaries we’ve been working on, which weave together expressions of liberation through art forms like poetry and dance.

“The whole idea is that it’s like a playground in search of strategies of liberation, using the festival as a way to explore different philosophies.

“John Mbiti explores the philosophy and spiritual understandings of time through the concept of Sasa na Zamani – in which the past informs everything that happens moving forward. That reflects how we constantly go back to pan-African histories to inform how we progress.”

Film-makers have been invited to submit films lasting up to 30 minutes from across genres, with no screening fees charged.

As well as submissions, the festival will feature documentaries produced by See My World. They include Homage, a “cinematic love letter to dance” that traces a culture through present-day portraits illustrating dance artists and archival material from Manchester, telling a story of joy, loss, migration, rhythm and resistance. Meanwhile, Poetic Justice explores how pan-African thought and Manchester’s poetry scene speak across decades.

Adekoya added: “The idea is that we would go against the norm of how film festivals are, because when we think about decolonisation, we think about how structures have been created to alienate and exclude communities.

“So we thought our film festival would look more at how we make film accessible and how stories that deserve to be seen get seen. Throughout the day we will have different activities, from exhibitions to explorations of our performances, discussions, Q&As, insights into directors’ processes, and workshops.

“We’ve been looking for literature and concepts that inform us and give us an understanding of who we truly are. And as works from thinkers like John Mbiti have come into our sphere, they have really emboldened us to think differently about our place in the world and what we do.”

See My World film festival runs from 2pm to 11pm on Saturday 21 November at Contact theatre, Oxford Road, Manchester.

world.title: Kenyan doomsday sect leader jailed for 200 years for murder of 190 children
world.snippet: Paul Mackenzie convicted over deaths of children and one adult after followers were ordered to starve themselves and their families The l...
world.content:
The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.

The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.

Prosecutors said Paul Mackenzie and his Good News International church ran ​a Christian doomsday sect whose members were ordered to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.

His accomplices threatened and beat victims to ensure they followed his orders. The emaciated bodies were found scattered in shallow graves and dumped in latrines. Some had been buried alive.

Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast in south-eastern Kenya.

In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered. Many were severely decomposed and only 26 could be identified.

Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument.

The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the forest more than three years ago.

It raised questions about how Mackenzie was able to continue operating despite being on the radar of the authorities since 2017, when police searched his premises.

In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated ‌to the Shakahola forest, police said.

The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.

Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic.

Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.

The plight of his followers began ​to emerge in March 2023, when a man told ​police his brother and wife had starved their children ​to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.

Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives said he brought forward the date ​on which he told his followers the ‌world would end. Police rearrested him and ​started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.

Last month’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into more than 200 other deaths are continuing.

Justice Diana Kavedza-Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.

Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths, including those of terrorism, which he has denied.

Prosecutors said that while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.
